1.1.intro: Work is an activity. A job is an agreed role in which someone does work under particular conditions, usually for pay. A career is the longer path formed by many roles and choices. An occupation names a broad kind of work; a position is a particular opening.
1.1.example: A neighborhood shop needs someone to serve customers on Saturdays. The shop offers wages and a schedule; the worker offers time, attention, and service. The same exchange appears in a laboratory, where a research assistant contributes skills and careful work.
1.1.language: The store is hiring a part-time assistant.
1.1.watch: A job is more than passion or salary. Look at the tasks, the agreement and the people involved.

1.2.intro: People work for different mixtures of reasons: income, security, independence, interest, belonging, growth or purpose. There is no moral requirement to be passionate about every employer. A reason can be genuine without being your complete life story.
1.2.example: Privately: “I need steady income.” In an application: “This role uses my customer-service experience and offers the schedule I am seeking.” Both can be true. The second helps the employer understand the fit.
1.2.language: I'm looking for stable work where I can use my experience.
1.2.watch: Never invent a mission-driven story just because you think interviewers want one.

1.3.intro: Employers hire because work must be done and the current team may lack enough time, capacity or expertise. A job description is the employer's attempt to name that missing contribution. Understanding the problem helps you select relevant evidence.
1.3.example: Northstar receives 200 customer requests a day but its team can answer only 150. A support hire could reduce the backlog. The employer needs listening, writing, organization and reliability—not a vague claim of enthusiasm.
1.3.language: You're looking for someone who can handle customer questions accurately.
1.3.watch: Some jobs require licenses or authorization, not just ability.

1.4.intro: Hiring is a decision made by two parties with incomplete information. A résumé shows selected history; an interview offers a conversation; a work sample shows a task. None perfectly predicts the future. Applicants also need information about pay, supervision, hours and safety.
1.4.example: The company wonders whether Maya can handle difficult customers. Maya wonders whether the evening shifts fit her studies. Both need answers before agreeing.
1.4.language: Could you tell me what the typical schedule looks like?
1.4.watch: The employer and applicant do not necessarily have equal bargaining power; a good process still respects both.

1.5.intro: Employers can evaluate specific examples more easily than unsupported adjectives. Evidence can come from work, school, volunteering, care responsibilities or personal projects. The point is to show what you did and what happened—not to exaggerate.
1.5.example: Weak: “I'm an excellent communicator.” Better: “I helped visitors find the right service desk and explained the process in English.” A student without paid work might describe coordinating a class project.
1.5.language: I organized the team schedule for our class project.
1.5.watch: If you cannot support a claim, describe what you are learning instead.

1.6.intro: The usual path is finding an opening, understanding requirements, applying, being screened, speaking with an employer, completing any assessment, receiving a decision and evaluating an offer. The order varies: some employers skip cover letters or combine interviews.
1.6.example: At Northstar, applicants submit a résumé, have a 15-minute recruiter call and complete one work-sample task before a conversation with the manager. Another employer might use only one interview.
1.6.language: I applied for the role and was invited to an interview.
1.6.watch: A hiring journey is a map, not a promise of a fixed sequence.

2.1.intro: A job title is only a label. To choose useful opportunities, inspect the actual duties, working hours, location, employment type and eligibility. Two “assistant” jobs can require completely different skills.
2.1.example: “Operations assistant” at Northstar involves tracking orders and scheduling staff. “Research assistant” at a university involves preparing data and lab notes. The shared word assistant tells you very little.
2.1.language: I'm looking for a part-time role with customer contact.
2.1.watch: Separate what you prefer from what you must have, such as work authorization or availability.

2.2.intro: Openings appear on employer career pages, job boards, campus sites, community networks, recruiting agencies and through introductions. Start with the actual employer and the posted role. A referral starts a conversation; it does not guarantee selection.
2.2.example: You see a job-board listing. Find the same opening on the company's career page, compare the title and deadline, then follow the official application instructions.
2.2.language: Where can I find the official job description?
2.2.watch: Avoid paying someone to guarantee a job or sharing sensitive documents with an unverified contact.

2.3.intro: Cold outreach is contacting someone who has not asked to hear from you. It can be appropriate for learning about a field, asking about a team or expressing interest in future openings. Make the request small, relevant and easy to refuse.
2.3.example: Instead of sending a stranger your full life story, ask a lab coordinator whether their group accepts applications from research assistants and link to a relevant project only if useful.
2.3.language: Would you be open to a brief question about your team's work?
2.3.watch: A cold message is not permission to demand referrals, insider information or repeated attention.

2.4.intro: A useful message tells the reader who you are, why you chose them and what modest next step you are requesting. Keep it brief and specific. One respectful follow-up after a reasonable interval can be appropriate; silence is also an answer.
2.4.example: Subject: Question about your support team. “Hello Jordan, I saw your team recently expanded customer support. I have experience handling walk-in requests. Could you point me to any open roles? Thank you, Maya.”
2.4.language: I came across your team's work on ... and had a brief question.
2.4.watch: Do not send identical flattering messages to dozens of people or follow up indefinitely.

2.5.intro: A job advertisement usually contains a role title, duties, essential requirements, preferred qualities, working arrangements and application steps. Read the duties first: they show what you would actually do. Then mark words you can support with evidence.
2.5.example: Northstar asks a support assistant to answer email requests, track cases and escalate difficult issues. This tells you the work matters more than the grand title.
2.5.language: The role involves responding to customer inquiries.
2.5.watch: Be careful with vague descriptions that omit pay, identity, duties or employment terms.

2.6.intro: An essential requirement is something the employer says you must have; a preferred qualification can improve fit but may not be mandatory. Some items—licenses, visas, legal working age—are hard eligibility constraints. If in doubt, ask rather than assume.
2.6.example: The advert says “English required; CRM experience preferred.” A candidate who writes clearly but has never used that exact system may still be worth considering; someone without required work permission cannot ignore that condition.
2.6.language: I meet the required language level, but I'm new to this software.
2.6.watch: Do not claim credentials you lack. And do not reject yourself solely for missing every preferred item.

2.7.intro: Research should answer concrete questions: What does the organization do? Who benefits? What would this team be responsible for? Are the employment terms credible? Use official pages, reliable outside sources and thoughtful questions.
2.7.example: Northstar says it helps small businesses manage deliveries. A support applicant can explain why accurate order updates matter to customers. The same research may reveal unclear conditions worth asking about.
2.7.language: I noticed your team works with small retailers.
2.7.watch: Praise is not research. Knowing a logo or slogan is not the same as understanding the work.

2.8.intro: Match a requirement with evidence from your experience. Think in three steps: employer need → your relevant action → what happened. If you lack direct experience, choose a genuine transferable example and name the remaining gap.
2.8.example: Need: track customer requests. Evidence: maintained a volunteer help-desk spreadsheet and followed up on open questions. This is not identical work, but the method transfers.
2.8.language: In my previous project, I tracked requests and followed up on unresolved issues.
2.8.watch: Use the employer's vocabulary only where it honestly describes your work.

2.9.intro: A good search balances relevance with reach. Spending hours customizing an application for a role you cannot legally take is wasteful; sending hundreds of generic applications can also be ineffective. Prioritize credible openings and allocate effort in proportion to fit and interest.
2.9.example: Compare three opportunities on duties, essential requirements, location, pay information and deadline. Choose one to investigate deeply and keep the others as options.
2.9.language: This role is a stronger fit because I can demonstrate two of its core duties.
2.9.watch: Quality matters, but no application guarantees an interview. Keep looking while you wait.
